title: Nekuda, sefira, partzuf: why the essential points of Tohu break, and how Tikun makes a person
overview:
Before the ten *sefiros* of *Atzilus*, the chapter brings in *nekuda*, *sefira* and *partzuf*: the difference between *Tohu* and *Tikun*. In *Tohu* each *sefira* is a point, the essence of an attribute before it spreads: a will for kindness that has a definition but no reason and no particular ways, like a person who is kind by nature, not one who read Dale Carnegie. Even its intellect and its *netzach* are the same point, all in one vessel, the *Akudim*.

So the *sefiros* of *Tohu* cannot join: two opposite essential goals allow no compromise, and whoever makes one of them the cure-all, "totally nice, always" or "get it yourself", fails. *Tikun* is the will for how to reach the goal. Kindness then depends on a reason, and one thing can be loved and hated at once, as G-d punished Shaul and ordered his eulogy at the same time. Only *Tikun* makes a *partzuf*, a person who sees the goal both sides share and takes the practical step, the way G-d mixed fire and water.

terms.gloss: the world of Chaos: each sefira only a point, an essential goal that cannot join its opposite
the world of Repair: each sefira divided into ten, so that they work together in harmony; the will for how to reach the goal
a point: the essence of an attribute before it spreads out, a bias with no reason and no particular ways
inclusion: the attributes working together like a harmony
the Name of forty-five: the abstract that a concrete form, BaN, comes to express
the Name of fifty-two: the concrete form, a vessel or an angel, that represents the abstract MaH
the bound ones: all ten sefiros included in one vessel, all one point
here: the point of Tohu even when divided into ten, each still a point, with no inclusion
lit. face: the stature of a person, the inclusion of all opposites; only in Tikun
composite kindness: kindness that depends on a reason, such as to one who did you a favor, weighed out by the situation
a middle: the place a thing loved from one side and hated from another ends up on one's list
a person of daas, who explains each of two opposite views better than its holder and finds the goal they share

sections.title: Before the sefiros of Atzilus: nekuda, sefira, partzuf, and the difference between Tohu and Tikun
sections.summary: Before the ten *sefiros* of *Atzilus* are explained one by one, the chapter brings in the three stages *nekuda*, *sefira* and *partzuf*. In *Tohu* each *sefira* is only a point; in *Tikun* each is divided into ten, and so they work together in harmony, through the Name *MaH*.

phrases.he: (כ) והנה קודם שיבואר ענין פרטי העשר ספירות דאצילות יש להקדים ענין נקודה ספירה פרצוף כו'
דהיות ידוע ההפרש שבין בחינת התהו לבחינת התיקון בכלל,
דעשר ספירות דתהו הן בבחינת נקודות לבד,
phrases.en: In *Tohu*, each *sefira* is like a *nekuda*.

phrases.he: שהן בבחינת הכתרים

blocks.text: Now he is going to start explaining about the *Keser* (crown). In this chapter he explains the general *inyan* (matter) of *nekudos*, *sefira* and *partzuf* (points, a single attribute, and a full stature of attributes), and of *Tikun* and *Tohu* (the worlds of Repair and of Chaos), so that we can understand how the *igulim* (circles) of *Atzilus* relate to the *yosher* (the straight line) of *Atzilus*. Before the details of the ten *sefiros* of *Atzilus* are explained, one has to bring in *nekuda*, *sefira*, *partzuf*.

It is known that there is a difference between *Tohu* and *Tikun* in general. **In *Tohu*, each *sefira* is like a *nekuda*.** What does it mean that it is like a *nekuda* (a point)? That it is not yet ten. As was explained in the last chapter, the association of your *etzem ratzon* (essential will) with a certain thing makes a bias, a leaning towards *chesed* (kindness) or a leaning another way. The bias to lean a certain way is just a point. It is not yet an actual, particular will for *chesed* or for anything else; it is just one point, that he leans towards *chesed*. But it is the general thing, and it becomes the source for every particular thing that will come out of it afterwards.

phrases.he: ובעולם התיקון הוא בבחינת התחלקות כל ספירה לי',
phrases.en: And then in *Tikun*, each *sefira* becomes already divided to ten.

phrases.he: על כן ממילא נעשה בחינת התיקון
phrases.en: and since each *sefira* is now diverse, it automatically makes it *Tikun*.

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת ההתכללות
phrases.en: That's the idea of *hiskalelus*, that it's like a harmony.

phrases.he: על ידי שם מ''ה כו'

blocks.text: In the world of *Tikun* each *sefira* is already divided into ten. And since each *sefira* is now diverse, that automatically makes it *Tikun*. *Tikun* has a lot of senses; here it means a harmony: the things work together. That is the idea of *hiskalelus* (inclusion): **it's like a harmony**.

This harmony comes through the Name *MaH* (the Name of forty-five). The relationship between the Name *MaH* and the Name *BaN* is always the same. Any concrete, set form, a *kli* (vessel) or an angel, when it is able to represent something abstract: the abstract thing is *MaH*, and the *kli* is *BaN*.

blocks.title: Letters make a vessel for an idea
blocks.text: For example, a language. The words are a tangible form. But through having a whole bunch of letters in different orders, you can make a *kli* in which an abstract idea can be expressed too. "So, he's going to explain now."

sections.title: The point: the essence of a midda before it spreads, a will for kindness with no reason
sections.summary: The *nekuda* is the essence of an attribute before it spreads out. It is not the essence as it is in the *yechida*, but the will for kindness once it is revealed: it already has a definition, but no reason and no particular ways of coming out.

phrases.he: וביאור הדברים ידוע שבחינת הנקודות הוא בחינת העצמיות טרם שמתפשט,
phrases.en: The *nekudos* is like the *etzem* before it spreads out,

phrases.he: כנקודה שהיא בלתי מתפשטת כו'
phrases.en: like a *nekuda* that doesn't come out yet.

blocks.text: The explanation: the *nekudos* are the *etzem* (essence) before it spreads out. It is like what was said before about the *igulim* and the *yosher*: the *igulim* are the way the soul is before it comes out into the body, and the *yosher* is the way it comes into the body. It is the same with *Tohu* and *Tikun*: the way it is in the *etzem*, and the way it comes out, the *hispashtus* (spreading forth). The point is **like a *nekuda* that doesn't come out yet**: as was said before, it is still within its *etzem hiyuli* (the raw, formless essence).

phrases.he: כמו אור מדת החסד,
phrases.en: for example, *chesed*,

phrases.he: הנה בחינת עצמיות דמדת החסד הוא בחינת הכתר שלו

blocks.text: Take, **for example, *chesed***. The essence of the attribute of *chesed* is its *Keser*. The *etzem* of the *midda* (attribute) of kindness is that a person has a desire for kindness, and that therefore he always leans to do things in a nice way.

phrases.he: ואמנם אין הכוונה על בחינת העצמיות דמדת החסד כמו שהוא נטוע ומושרש בעצם הנפש שנקרא יחידה
phrases.en: But we're not talking here about the *etzem* like it is in the *yechida*,

phrases.he: כנזכר לעיל, שהוא בחינת היולי לגמרי (כנזכר לעיל באות יו''ד וי''א)
אלא הכוונה הוא על בחינת גלוי הרצון לדבר חסד פרטי
phrases.en: We're talking about now when a person has a particular *ratzon* for doing an actual kind thing.

phrases.he: מן העלם חסד העצמיות ההיולי

blocks.text: But we are not talking here about the essence of the attribute of *chesed* as it is planted and rooted in the essence of the soul, called the *yechida* (the essence of the soul), where it is entirely *hiyuli* (raw potential). That would correspond to before the *tzimtzum* (contraction), as was said above in chapters 10 and 11.

We are talking about the revelation of the will for a particular thing of *chesed*, out of the hidden, *hiyuli* kindness of the essence: when a person has a particular *ratzon* (will) for doing an actual kind thing. In *Adam Kadmon* they created a *ratzon* to be a nice person. The essential *midda* of *chesed* created the will to be a nice person; in *Adam Kadmon* they create a picture of what it means to be a nice person; and now that picture makes them have particular *ratzonos* (wills) to do nice things.

The *etzem* of all the particular nice things they are doing is still one *nekuda*: that they see these things as being nice. The *etzem* comes over into it. Even though it has now become connected to a certain form, because of *Adam Kadmon*, and *chesed* now has a definition, so that "you can look it up in a dictionary what *chesed* is", the *nekuda* that you just want to do whatever is nice is still there.

phrases.he: שגם זה הרצון
phrases.en: even this particular *ratzon*, that you want to do a nice thing,

phrases.he: הוא בלתי התפשטות עדיין
רק כמו שהוא בלא טעם כלל
phrases.en: this is without any reason at all,

phrases.he: לרצון זה, למה רוצה בגלוי לחסד זה כו'
ומכל שכן שאין בו בחינת התחלקות אופנים שונים
phrases.en: and he definitely didn't yet think up particular ways of exactly what he wants to do.

blocks.text: Even this particular will, that you want to do a nice thing, is still without *hispashtus*: you have a particular definition of what it means to be nice, but nothing particular yet. So what are you going to do? You have to see, according to the situation, exactly what particular things will come out of it. It is like a normal person who knows what it means to be nice, and is a nice person: he has a bias and a leaning towards kindness. But right now nothing is coming up, so he is not doing anything.

And **this is without any reason at all**: why he wants this kindness in the open. It is not that there is a certain situation, and therefore he wants it in order to accomplish some goal. His goal is the *chesed*. That is his *etzem*, it is the *nekuda*, that is what he is after: because of his *etzem*, he likes that.

blocks.title: Dale Carnegie's book
blocks.text: It is not like a person who wants to be nice to people because he understands that if he wants to be successful in his career he has to be nice to people. He read Dale Carnegie's book, *How to Win Friends and Influence People*, so he wants to be nice to people. That is not his *ratzon*. The *nekuda* of his *ratzon* is not to be nice; the *nekuda* of his *ratzon* is to make money, or whatever it is.

But a person who by his *etzem*, his nature, is *chafetz chesed* (desires kindness) wants to be kind. Therefore he created a self-image of a kind person, and his goal in life, or at least part of it, is to be a kind, caring person. The effect of having such an *Adam Kadmon* is that he has this constant *nekuda*, that he wants to do kind things.

And all the more so it has no division into different ways. If it does not have a reason, so that he is not doing it as a means to another end, he **definitely didn't yet think up particular ways of exactly what he wants to do**. He does not really have a will for doing such and such; he has a will for whatever will be kind. It is not yet limited to particular instances.

blocks.title: A will for money, from any deal
blocks.text: On the other hand, if somebody had an *etzem ratzon* for money: that essential will does not really care how he is going to get the money. He just wants the money. He does not care if it comes from a business deal like this or like that. The same here: the guy just wants the *chesed*. He does not care how it is going to come out.

sections.title: Intellect and victory inside the point: all one point, the Akudim in one vessel
sections.summary: Even the bias of the intellect towards kindness, the *chachma* of that *chesed*, and its *netzach* are only the same point. The ten are there, but with no recognizable division: this is the world of *Akudim*, all in one *kli*.

phrases.he: או גם אם שכלו מטה כלפי חסד דווקא, אין בו התחלקות אופנים שונים
אף על פי ששכל הנוטה בעצם לחסד ולזכות, הוא בחינת חכמה שבחסד העצמי, אבל גם הוא רק בבחינת נקודה

blocks.question: "Wait a minute": because of this essential will, his intellect too is biased towards kindness. So that is a *chachma*, and there is already a division in the point, the will and then the bias in the intellect?
blocks.text: This too is a *nekuda*. It is not an actual *sechel* (intellect) yet. Because of the *etzem ratzon* his *sechel* will always lean towards being liberal and kind, to look at things with a good eye; but that bias is part of the same point, and it has no division into different ways.

The intellect that leans in its essence to kindness and to merit is the *chachma* (wisdom) of the essential *chesed*, but it too is only a point. Everywhere, even in *Tohu*, you can divide it up: it includes ten, and each of the ten includes ten. So you can find a *chachma* there. But it is really the same *nekuda*, that he wants *chesed*: therefore his *chachma* wants *chesed* and his *middos* (emotional attributes) want *chesed*. Everything leans towards *chesed*. They are all in the way of a point, because it does not yet have to do with any particular situation. Whatever situation will come up, he already has this bias, this leaning.

phrases.he: וכן נצח שבחסד זה
phrases.en: that he's going to want to overcome any opposition to any *chesed*.

phrases.he: הוא בא בבחינת נקודה
ונמצא דגם שבחינת החסד העצמי הבא בגלוי כלול מי', רצון ושכל ומדות, אבל אין בהם התחלקות ניכרת
phrases.en: even though really, technically, it does have ten, you could divide it up into ten *sefiros*, there's no recognizable distinction

phrases.he: אלא כולן בבחינת נקודה אחד,
phrases.en: they're all in one *nekuda*,

phrases.he: והוא בחינת העקודים, שעקודים היו בכלי אחד כו'
phrases.en: This is the level of *Akudim*, where really all of the ten *sefiros* are included in one *kli*,

blocks.text: So too the *netzach* (victory) of this *chesed*: **that he's going to want to overcome any opposition to any *chesed***. He will want to fight for it. He has not yet figured out what is in his way, so that he would want to fight it; but in theory, if there were something in his way, he would want to fight it. It is a *nekuda* that is halfway, and it too comes as a point.

So the essential *chesed* that comes into the open includes ten, will and intellect and *middos*, but there is no recognizable division among them. even though really, technically, it does have ten, and you could divide it up into ten *sefiros*, there is no recognizable distinction, because they are all really the same *nekuda*. It is all just that he wants *chesed*, and therefore everything together is going to go to *chesed*.

Rather, **they're all in one *nekuda***. **This is the level of *Akudim***, the bound ones: really all ten *sefiros* are included in one *kli*. He wants *chesed*, and that is the meaning of all of them: his *ratzon*, his *sechel*, his *middos* are all right now the same thing, that he wants *chesed*. That is the only meaning or definition there is, and it does not really matter which one you are talking about; they are all the same *nekuda*. It is just his goal, his final goal.

sections.title: Sefira: the sefiros of Tohu cannot join, and two opposite goals cannot compromise
sections.summary: Because each *sefira* of *Tohu* is an essential goal, they cannot unite: one reigns and dies, then the next. Two opposite essential wills cannot be mixed or compromised, and a person or a society that makes one of them the cure-all fails; so too Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel could not convince each other.

phrases.he: ולזה בחינת עשר ספירות דתהו הן בלתי מתיחדין ומתכללין זה עם זה
phrases.en: And therefore the *sefiros* of *Tohu* do not unite or include with each other at all,

phrases.he: אלא הן זה תחת זה
phrases.en: they're one under the other,

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב וימלוך וימת כו'

blocks.text: Therefore the ten *sefiros* of *Tohu* do not unite or include with each other at all. They are one under the other, as it says, "and he reigned, and he died", of each of the kings of *Tohu*: the kings of Esav, which represent the kings of *Tohu*.

phrases.he: כמו רצון העצמי שבא בגלוי חסד
הגם שכלול בו שכל כו', לא יתחבר עם רצון עצמי היפוכו הבא בבחינת הדין

blocks.text: So the essential will that comes out as *chesed*, even though intellect is included in it, will not join with its opposite essential will, which comes as *din* (judgement). Even though a guy has an *etzem ratzon* for *chesed*: you see this kind of thing very much in politics, that for whatever reason one person has liberal leanings and another person has conservative leanings.
You see it with any kind of thing people believe in. It is really a belief, an *etzem nekuda* they are connected to, like people with missionaries and the like: they believe whatever it is.

sensitivity.reason: Holds up missionaries as the type of believer whose reasoning is only a front for a fixed belief.
sensitivity.publishable: You see it with any kind of thing people believe in. It is really a belief, an *etzem nekuda* they are connected to: they believe whatever it is.

blocks.text: Because of this they are willing to come into *sechel* to try to convince you. Both sides will come into *sechel*. But the *sechel* is not really *sechel*; it is really *ratzon*, it is still their belief. So you could talk to one of these guys till you are blue, and you are never going to convince him of anything, because it is a one-way *sechel*. To them *sechel* is a puppet, to convince you of what they believe.

That is not necessarily a bad thing; this is the way it starts off. *Sechel* was originally built for this: on this level, that is what *sechel* does. It just interprets and expresses to somebody else what you believe. But it is not able to convince somebody whose *etzem nekuda* is somewhere else.
This is also why, whenever you come to a thing like this, like in Israel with the Jews and the Arabs, because it is a religious thing, democracy does not work.

sensitivity.reason: A political opinion on the conflict between Jews and Arabs in Israel and on democracy there.

blocks.text: You cannot tell two people to sit down and compromise if their inner goals are in conflict. When it comes to things on the side of the goal, then you can make a compromise. But when it comes to the actual goal itself, there is no room to compromise, because my *etzem ratzon* is the exact opposite of your *etzem ratzon*. It is not a matter of "Well, you can tell me that if I do this, then I'll get what I want." That is the way you make a compromise: we want two different things, but if we figure out some thing that we can do to our mutual benefit, we agree to do it, because then we both gain.

But what happens if the issue is the thing itself, say it comes between one guy's life and the other guy's life? You cannot say, "Well, make a compromise." You cannot do that. It is an all-or-nothing deal. And it is the same within a person himself: from the side of these essential wills, you can only really have one at a time.

blocks.title: Totally nice, always
blocks.text: Some people kind of live in *Tohu*, in the *igulim*. They lock on to *chesed* and say, "That's it, I'm going to be totally nice, always." Kindness is their goal. If a person does not have a mature view, he will not realize that sometimes, to accomplish *chesed*, you have to do something that is outwardly *gevura* (might, restraint), even when *chesed* is your real goal; and that is the *inyan* of *Tikun*. Such a person will just try to be totally, altruistically nice, which is his ultimate goal; he would like to be like that all the time. And then he gets stepped on, and eventually it does not work. Or a person will try to do that for a country, or a classroom, anything: eventually it fails, and so it dies.

blocks.title: "Get it yourself"
blocks.text:
Then the person says, "Oh, so now I'm going to do *gevura*." But he is going to do *gevura* also in the way of *Tohu*. Now anybody who asks him to pass the salt, he says, "Get it yourself." Everything is totally *gevura*. There is a *maala* (an advantage) to doing things that way, to making people work and so on; but if you are going to be completely "only get what you deserve", that is also not going to work, and so that also dies.

And so with every single one of these things: if a person or a society took one of them and tried to make it the cure-all, it would not work. And it is only possible to have one at a time, because in their essence they contradict each other.

phrases.he: (כמחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל וכהאי גוונא,
דגם שמנגדו יקשה עליו
phrases.en: even if the opposition will ask questions to him,

phrases.he: ולא יוכל למצוא טעם
phrases.en: and he's not able to find an explanation,

phrases.he: ישתוק,
phrases.en: he'll be quiet,

phrases.he: אבל לא יוכל להודות ולחזור בו,
phrases.en: he's not able to admit and then change his mind,

phrases.he: להתכלל בדעה שמנגדו כלל כו')
phrases.en: to the opposite opinion at all.

blocks.text: Like the dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel. Why did they not convince each other? They were reasonable people. The reason is that their dispute came from an essential difference, not from the side of the *sechel*: it came from the essential root of their souls, which is like a *Tohu* type of thing. But they were in holiness, and that is why this is in parentheses: it is not a full example.

Because once they decided the *halacha* (the law), each one did as the *halacha* was decided, whichever way that was. From the side of their essential leaning they were biased to see things a certain way, to deal with things a certain way. But they had a deeper connection to Torah, and so if the Torah says to do it like this, even though they did not see it that way, they would still do it.

So **even if the opposition will ask questions to him**, and **he's not able to find an explanation, he'll be quiet**. He will just say, "I don't know." But he will not be able to turn back on his opinion, because his opinion is not really based on a logical consideration; he essentially perceives things a certain way. The *sechel* is just trying to find the right words. This is really the way it works in Torah: they perceive it in spirituality, and then they are just trying to find the right words to express it, to bring it into human intellect. But human intellect is not really its root.

But **he's not able to admit and then change his mind** and agree **to the opposite opinion at all**. He is not at all able to concede. The reason is that each one has a certain point which is an essential thing, and *eilu v'eilu divrei Elokim chaim* ("these and these are the words of the living G-d"), so there is no reason that they should concede.

sections.title: Tikun: the midda spreads out of its essence, into a will for how to reach the goal
sections.summary: In *Tikun* the attribute comes out of its point: it is no longer about the goal but about how to accomplish it in a particular case. Then kindness depends on a reason, like kindness to one who did you a favor, and it is a composite kindness; so too the composite judgement of a kind man toward his enemy.

phrases.he: אבל בחינת התיקון היינו כאשר המדה בא מבחינת נקודה שלה להתפשטות חוץ מן העצמיות רצון ושכל שבה

blocks.text: But *Tikun* is when the *midda* comes out of its point into *hispashtus*, outside its essence, will and intellect. Now we are not dealing with your *etzem ratzon*, not talking about your goal. "Okay, whatever your goal is, forget about the goal." Now we are talking about how to accomplish your goal.

When it comes to your essential goal, this is the thing of religion. Religion is about ultimate truths: the ultimate reality, and the ultimate goal of a person and of the world. So there can only be one truth. You cannot have pluralism in religion.

blocks.title: Going to New York by way of the south
blocks.text: But when it comes to the means to accomplish it, you have to recognize this. If you are trying to travel somewhere, you have to know your destination, and that you cannot change. You can only be going to one place at once: if you are going to New York, you cannot be going to Chicago, you have to pick. But sometimes, in order to get somewhere north, you have to go south, to go around something. So it is a whole separate *ratzon*. A person who wants to go to a certain place and just starts going in that direction is going to come up against all these walls and things in his way. That is not the best way to do it.

blocks.title: The short long way and the long short way
blocks.text: Like that story with the long short way and the short long way. The guy wanted to get to the palace. He can go the short long way: just go straight, and end up very close, but there is a wall in front of him and he cannot actually get into the palace. So it was really short, but it is long, because it is impossible to get in. The long short way means being willing to compromise and go a slow route; but it is short, because you are actually getting there. Like they say, shortcuts make for long delays. If a person tries to make clever schemes with these kinds of things, it is not worth it.
So this is the *inyan* of *Tikun*: we are no longer dealing with the *etzem ratzon*, but with the *ratzon* for how to accomplish it in a particular instance.

phrases.he: דהיינו כמו מדת החסד כאשר יולד הרצון ושכל להטות כלפי חסד לזולתו
מצד שעשה לו טובה
phrases.en: You want to be nice to somebody because he did you a favor.

phrases.he: ולא מצד בחינת עצם הטוב הבא בגלוי בהכרח מטבע הטוב שבעצמיות נפשו
אדרבה יוכל להיות אכזרי בטבע,
phrases.en: The person could be cruel naturally.

phrases.he: ולמי שחננו והצילו ממות
phrases.en: But to somebody that saved his life, that did a lot of kindness to him and saved his life,

phrases.he: וכהאי גוונא
ירצה להטיב,
phrases.en: for that person he's going to always be gracious,

phrases.he: ויטה שכלו עליו תמיד לחסד וזכות
phrases.en: and he's always going to be biased to look at them favorably.

phrases.he: כו' וכהאי גוונא

blocks.text: For example, the attribute of *chesed*, when the will and the intellect to lean towards kindness to another are born because he did him a favor. We are not talking about being kind because in your essence you want always to be kind to everybody. **You want to be nice to somebody because he did you a favor.** Your real goal is not that you just want to be kind to everybody all the time.

Let us say the guy wants his personal happiness, or money, or whatever it is. If a guy is helping him out, he is going to want to be kind to this person; the *sechel* is that it will help him out more in the future. Or maybe he just has an essential thing of gratitude, so once the guy does it, he will be kind to him. But he is not acting this way to everybody. He does not believe that you should always be completely nice to everybody; it depends what the person does. You should be nice to people who are nice to you; to people who are not nice to you, you should not be nice.

And not from the essential good and kindness that comes out necessarily from the good nature in the essence of his soul. From the side of the essential attribute of *chesed*, he has to be nice to everybody, because that is his nature, and it does not matter what the person did to him or not.

On the contrary, **the person could be cruel naturally**. **But to somebody that saved his life, that did a lot of kindness to him**, he is going to want to do good, **he's going to always be gracious** to him, **and he's always going to be biased to look at them favorably**. Now he has connected his *etzem ratzon* to that person, but how much he is connected depends on what the person did for him: the more kindness a person does for you, the more you connect your *ratzon* to him. That is a very different type of thing, because now it becomes complicated: when are you nice and when are you not nice? This is called the *ratzon murkav* (the composite will), as he is going to say now.

phrases.he: שזה נקרא חסד וטוב המורכב,
phrases.en: this is called a complex or composite kindness and good.

phrases.he: ולא חסד פשוט ועצמי
phrases.en: it's not the same simple thing for everybody

phrases.he: שמצד הטבע כלל
וכהאי גוונא יובן בהיפוכו,
phrases.en: the same way with the opposite,

phrases.he: במדת הדין המורכב, להטות רצונו ושכלו כלפי חוב לשונאו שעשה לו רעה הרבה,
גם שבעצם טבעו הוא איש חסדן ורחמן כו'
phrases.en: even if *b'etzem* he's a kind person,

blocks.text: It is what the text calls **a complex or composite kindness and good**, *chesed hamurkav*. It is complex because it has a lot of parts, and a lot depends: you have to weigh out the situation. It is not a simple and essential *chesed*, coming from nature; **it's not the same simple thing for everybody**.

It is understood the same way with the opposite, the composite attribute of judgement: to bend his will and intellect towards guilt for his enemy, who did him a lot of harm. If somebody was very mean to a person and did a lot of bad to him, he is going to become his enemy. But this does not mean that the person is a cruel guy, **even if *b'etzem* he's a kind person**, compassionate. It could be that by his essential nature a person likes to be kind, and that is really what he would want; but he has to realize that there are certain people you should not be nice to.

If a person made the *midda* of *chesed* his whole *metzius* (existence), he would be able to say, "Well, even if I'm gonna get killed for it, I'm going to be nice to somebody, even if it's gonna bite me back." But when you go up to the *pnimiyus* (the inner side), even within *Tohu* there is the head, the inner will they are coming from. And so *Tikun* really has a higher *shoresh* (root).

blocks.title: The parent who wants to be loved
blocks.text: Take a parent who wants to just be nice to the kids and to have a relationship of love. So he wants to be outwardly kind, so that the kids will reciprocate and show appreciation and love. That is what he wants: to be loved by the kids, and so he just does things the kids will see as kind. But that does not necessarily mean that he really wants to be kind. If you go deeper and appreciate that the inner side of the will to be kind is for their benefit, and you really want that, then you will be willing to do something that outwardly looks like *gevura*, depending on the *sechel*.

sections.title: In the composite, opposites can live together: love and hate, Shaul, Shlomo and the Flood
sections.summary: Once the attributes are tied to a thing through a reason, one thing can be loved from one side and hated from another, and a middle is weighed out between them. So G-d punished and honored Shaul at once, was angry and joyful over Shlomo, and found in man's evil inclination both a reason to destroy and a reason to spare: in *Tikun*, in the actual world, nothing is pure.

phrases.he: ועל דרך זה יובן שיוכל להיות במורכב כמה מיני אופנים שונים
phrases.en: once you start having these considerations, it can come out in many different ways

phrases.he: מאד, לפי אופן דבר שמורכב בו המדות
phrases.en: according to the considerations that you're using to put together the *middos*.

phrases.he: כמו אהבה ושנאה
התלויים בדבר
phrases.en: that are dependent on something,

phrases.he: כנזכר לעיל
הרי יוכל למצוא דבר שמצדו א' יאהבנו, ויהיה רצונו ושכלו הכל לטוב וחסד, ומצדו הב' באותו הדבר עצמו, ישנאנו ויטה רצונו ושכלו לרע ועונש

blocks.text: In this way it is understood that the composite can come in many very different ways: **once you start having these considerations, it can come out in many different ways**, **according to the considerations that you're using to put together the *middos***. Like love and hate **that are dependent on something**: one can find a thing which from one side he loves, and his will and intellect are all for good and kindness, and from the second side, in the very same thing, he hates it, and his will and intellect lean to bad and punishment.

Once you let your essential *middos* be connected to something on the basis of a *sechel*, then from one consideration it is beneficial to me and from another consideration it is bad for me. From this side I love it; from that side I hate it.

blocks.title: Drugs and their side effects
blocks.text: For example, drugs and things like that. On the one hand people like them, because they are pleasurable and do things that feel good for them; on the other hand they hate them because of what they do to them, the negative side effects. They love the positive effects and hate the negative effects. Since we are talking about an actual thing in the world, this physical thing has both of these connected to it. You cannot have one without the other.

Once both are connected to that one thing, your *sechel* can associate two opposite *middos* with it: from this side you will like it, from that side you will hate it. And then you have to decide which one is going to override the other in practice, and how to act.

phrases.he: עד שיוכל להיות בחינת ממוצע
phrases.en: until you come out with a *memutza*

phrases.he: כלול מחסד וגבורה יחד

blocks.text: Until there can be a *memutza* (a middle), including *chesed* and *gevura* together. What you like, you totally like; what you hate, you totally hate. But now, practically, you have to say: "Well, this is going to end up somewhere in the middle of my list of things that I like, because on the one hand I like it, but on the other hand it's bad." So practically you are able to prioritize. Essentially there is no mixing: what you like you like, and what you do not like you do not like.

blocks.title: Profit and expenses in a business deal
blocks.text: But since we are talking about the way it comes out in an actual physical thing, where both are together, you can do a simple equation of the total amount of gain: measure the amount of pleasure against the amount of pain, subtract, and figure out how to maximize. Like in a business deal: you want the profit and you do not want the expenses. You can have a business deal where you make some money from selling something, but the money you have to put into it makes you lose more than you gain, so it is not worth it. Or you could gain a little bit, or you could gain a lot.

blocks.title: Only a deal that is profitable enough
blocks.text: The money you are gaining back is always what you want. But since you are acting according to *sechel*, you can say, "I'm not just going to go to any deal that's going to end up making somebody give me money. I'm only going to do one that's going to end up being profitable, and it has to be profitable enough to be meeting my needs." So you end up making a hierarchy, that you like this better than that, and something you think of as a *memutza*: this one is so-so.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב באשר משפטו שם כו'
על שאול שהמית את הגבעונים ועל שלא נספד כהלכה,
דבר והיפוכו כאחד

blocks.text: As it is written, *ba'asher mishpato sham* ("I forget how the end of the word is"). The *inyan* is that when *Hashem* is judging, there you find His compassion and His *chesed*. So it seems like opposite things.

blocks.title: Shaul punished and eulogized
blocks.text: This was said about Shaul, who killed the Givonim, and about his not being eulogized as he should have been: one thing and its opposite at once. Shaul was punished because he killed the Givonim, who had helped Dovid. Because of what Shaul did there was a plague, and Dovid did not know what to do; through prophecy they found out that it was because of Shaul. So Dovid was told to give over some of Shaul's descendants to the Givonim to be hung, and in that way they were punishing Shaul. But at the same time that Dovid was told to give these people over to the Givonim, he was told to make a *hesped* (eulogy) for Shaul, because he had never been given proper honor.

So wait a minute: is G-d mad at Shaul, or is He happy with Shaul? He is punishing him and rewarding him at the same time. The *inyan* is that it was not an essential thing, that G-d hates Shaul and that is it, or that He likes him. It is like a parent who gets mad at a child and yells at him for doing something wrong: it is not that now he does not love him anymore. What you do that is good, I like, and what you do that is not good, I do not like. They have no direct connection to each other, so you can have both at the same time.

phrases.he: וכן כשנשא שלמה בת פרעה,
phrases.en: also with *Shlomo*, that *Hashem* was angry because he married *Bas Paroh*,

phrases.he: על זה אמר כי על אפי כו'
phrases.en: that this is: I'm angry,

phrases.he: ושיר השירים נאמר על שמחת בנין בית המקדש
וכמו שכתוב ביום שמחת לבו כו'
phrases.en: the day of the rejoicing of his heart, which is the time the *Beis HaMikdash* was built,

phrases.he: שמחה וחרון אף, דבר והיפוכו כאחד
phrases.en: So we see that *Hashem* both had *simcha* and anger at *Shlomo* at the same time.

blocks.text: So too with Shlomo: *Hashem* was angry because he married *Bas Paroh* (Pharaoh's daughter). Of that He said *ki al api*, "**I'm angry**"; He said, "I was angry about that forever." But at the same time, *Shir HaShirim* (the Song of Songs) was said on the joy of the building of the *Beis HaMikdash* (the Temple): since Shlomo built the *Beis HaMikdash*, it says *Shir HaShirim*, which is a whole thing of *simcha* (joy) and love, how much *Hashem* loved Shlomo. As it is written, "on the day of the rejoicing of his heart", the time the *Beis HaMikdash* was built, *Hashem* was eternally happy because of it. Joy and burning anger, one thing and its opposite at once: *Hashem* had both *simcha* and anger at Shlomo at the same time.

phrases.he: וכן כי יצר לב האדם רע וכו'
phrases.en: and the same thing with man

phrases.he: ומתחלה אמר וירא יהו״ה כי רבה רעת האדם כו' וינחם כו'
phrases.en: First, before the flood, it says G-d saw how bad man was, and He regretted making man.

blocks.text: And **the same thing with man**: with the *Mabul* (the Flood), first G-d said that since man is bad, we are going to destroy him. After the *Mabul* He said that since man is bad, we will not destroy him. So what do you mean? The same fact, that man has a *yetzer hara* (evil inclination), was both a reason to hate him and a reason to have mercy on him.

blocks.title: Both sides of a court case
blocks.text: Why? One side is saying, "Well, they're bad, so we should get rid of them." The other side is saying, "Yeah, but they're born bad, so it's not their fault." This is like what happens in a court case: on the same *nekuda*, one side shows you how it connects to *chesed*, and the other side shows you how it connects to *gevura*. One side says, "They're born bad, so we should get rid of them, because that's a bad thing: they're going to sin." The other side says, "Yeah, but that means it's not their fault, because they're born bad, so we should be easy on them." The first side says, "No, that makes them worse. That means there's even no hope." You could look at it both ways; it really just depends. Whatever you want, you will be able to use that as an excuse for it.

blocks.title: Why the rainbow came after the Flood
blocks.text: At the end of the day, before the *Mabul* the bad could not be refined, and after the *Mabul* the world was refined a little, which is why there could be a rainbow. In a rainbow, the cloud obstructs the light. Before the *Mabul* the atmosphere was thick and would not make a rainbow. After the *Mabul* the atmosphere became thinner, so the light was able to come through, and when it hit the raindrops it would make a rainbow. It revealed the hidden beauty in the light, through that resistance.

blocks.title: Why the rainbow came after the Flood
blocks.text: So after the *Mabul* the bad of a person was refined enough that it could be used for good: a person can overcome his *yetzer hara*, and the fact that he has to fight, that he has an opposition and it is hard for him to do what G-d wants, will bring out the inner beauty of his connection to G-d, of his *nefesh Elokis* (G-dly soul). So then it was a good thing. Before the *Mabul* it could not be used in a positive way, and therefore the bad side won.
And at first, before the *Mabul*, it says that G-d saw how bad man was, and He regretted making man.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב במקום אחר
שזהו מבחינת המדות דתיקון,
phrases.en: the fact that you can have both *middos* for the same thing is because it's in *Tikun*,

phrases.he: שהם בבחינת מורכבים
phrases.en: which are complex.

phrases.he: דהיינו בהתפשטות דבר
phrases.en: that you're dealing not with a theory.

phrases.he: שלא מצד העצמיות לבד
על כן יוכל להיות התכללות דבר והיפוכו כו'
phrases.en: Therefore, you can have two opposite things,

blocks.text: As is explained in a *maamar* (discourse), this comes from the *middos* of *Tikun*: **the fact that you can have both *middos* for the same thing is because it's in *Tikun***, where they are composite. That is, in the *hispashtus* of the thing: you are dealing not with a theory. In theory you can have pure things, but when it comes out in practice you can never have something pure. Everything has a benefit and a detriment in it, something you could see as good and something you could see as bad. There is no physical thing that is going to be completely pleasurable or completely painful.

blocks.title: All the powers of the soul in one body
blocks.text: So once you are talking about something in the *hispashtus*, in the physical world, everything comes together there. It is like the way the soul comes into the body: there the body separates each power, and you see how it has all the different powers of the soul in one place. You have the seeing and the hearing and all these things, and they are all connected together in one body. And that is the way any physical thing has all the different *sefiros* and *middos* in one: they all get put into the one thing, in different proportions, so that it is not found as only itself alone.

blocks.title: No light without a little darkness
blocks.text: **Therefore, you can have two opposite things**, one thing and its opposite included together. In theory, light and darkness are opposites, or sweet and bitter. In theory they are complete opposites, and one totally contradicts the other. In practice, though, you can never find something that is not a mixture of both. There is no such thing as pure light that is only bright: you could always make it brighter, which means there is a little darkness there.

sections.title: Tohu stays a sefira; only Tikun makes a partzuf, a person, like fire and water mixed
sections.summary: Even divided into ten, the point of *Tohu* is only a *sefira*, not the *partzuf* of a person who includes all opposites. A person, and *Tikun*, sees the deeper goal both sides share and works it out in practice, without dropping the goal; as *Sefer Yetzira* says, G-d mixed fire and water, not in their essence but as composites.

phrases.he: והיינו בחינת נקודה דתהו,
דגם כשנעשה בהתחלקות לי', אין זה רק ספירה
phrases.en: Even in *Tohu*, when it divides up into a *sefira*, and it has ten *sefiros*, they're also *nekudos*.

blocks.text: This is the point of *Tohu*, the essential *middos*. The essence of *Tohu* is *Akudim*, a *nekuda*, one point. **Even in *Tohu*, when it divides up into a *sefira*, and it has ten *sefiros*, they're also *nekudos***. So it is not really *hiskalelus*. In *Tohu* the *gevura* is really all *chesed*: it is all one *sefira*, meaning that the *chesed* takes the *gevura* and makes it also a *chesed*.

blocks.title: Even more reason to be nice to him
blocks.text: Like the guys who lean towards *chesed*. You tell them, "Well, this guy is so bad, look at all the bad things he did," and they say, "Oh, so that's even more of a reason that we should be nice to him. Look, poor person," like people say, "he's a victim" and everything. They turn anything into a *chesed*.

Because it is a *sefira*: a guy who in his essence believes a certain way, or wants something a certain way, from the side of his *emuna* (faith) or of his will. Then you can have a person who will deliberately come and talk to you, who is already willing to go out and talk, to missionize; but it is still really only one *sefira*. Like the *Akudim* of *Tohu*. They are not really considering the other side at all.

You can see the sign of this a lot. A person who is in the way of *Tohu* is trying to make his whole *partzuf* out of one *sefira*. But that is not really the real *etzem*. The real *etzem* includes all ten, and so he should be able to have all ten together. And with a person who cannot get to that, you see a very big *shtarkeit* (fierceness): a fierce opposition to the opposite, because he feels it threatens him, his *inyan*.

*Tikun* requires a deeper look. In the next chapter he is going to explain about the middle *kav* (line), how it is able to connect opposites. If there are two opposite opinions, one guy has the *chesed* side and totally, vehemently opposes the *gevura* side; the *gevura* guy has the *gevura* view and vehemently opposes the *chesed* view; and they see the other side as completely evil and wrong and subversive and everything.

But that is the *inyan* of a *bar daas* (a person of *daas*), as the Frierdiker Rebbe (the previous Lubavitcher Rebbe) describes in a *maamar*, the *inyan* of *daas* (knowledge): he takes these two people with two opposite views and says, "I'm going to explain to both of you what your view is, better than you understand it." He shows them the real depth and peels it off. He shows that you do not really want a particular instance of *chesed*: he explains to them what the real *etzem ratzon* of *chesed* is, before it becomes associated with a certain deed, whatever level you are talking about. He brings it up a step.

When you bring it up a step, you realize: so why do you really want *chesed*? What is the theory behind *chesed*? He says: "Every person has in him a little bit of good. The reason you would lean towards letting the person off is that you appreciate that there is that good in the person, and you want to bring it out so that it will be expressed." That is the main *nekuda*. And then it will be brought out, to help himself and other people.

What is the thing of *gevura*? You say, "Yeah, but it doesn't matter what's inside, that he means well or that he has potential. If it doesn't come out into deed, into the external things he does, then it's worthless." So then he says, "Well, really you both want the same thing. You both want the inner good to come out and be expressed externally. That's really what you both want. So now we have to decide what's the best way to get there. What is the best way to get this person to bring out his inner good?"

Is it by telling him how he is really good, that we really love him and appreciate his value as a person, or by telling him that we expect more? Which side should we focus on? Should we be strict and tell him he is not doing good enough, we expect more of him, or should we tell him that we appreciate his potential? It depends what type of person you are talking to. It depends on the nature of the person. So you are willing to do whatever it is, because you realize that for your real goal it does not really matter which one you do; it matters which one works.

blocks.title: Live and let live, or sit down together
blocks.text: In order to get the *middos* of *Tohu* really into *Tikun*: you can have a *Tikun* that comes after a *midda* of *Tohu* which is like a *reshus harabim* (a public domain). It is kind of like in America: everybody really has his own *ratzon* and its opposites, but we just make sure that people do not go around killing people who have opposite views. So everybody goes around, and they are able to relate in things that do not touch their essential will.

But a real *Tikun* means that you are able to actually have two people sit down and work together. To do that, you have to find their real, deeper goal, a common goal that transcends both of their particular things. That is a real *Tikun*. But in *Tohu*, even when it comes out, it only becomes a *sefira*, not a *partzuf*.

phrases.he: ולא פרצוף אדם,
phrases.en: It's not a person.

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת ההתכללות מכל ההפכים כו'

blocks.text: Not the *partzuf* of a person. It is not a person: you are talking to a wall still. The *inyan* of a person is the inclusion of all opposites.

That is a thing you see a lot of times with *baalei teshuva* (returnees to Judaism). If they are not given proper instruction, it is very easy for them to end up not being a person. Their whole approach to religion is a thing of *emuna*, and they feel a big, passionate drive for altruism. If a person connects that to just one aspect of the truth, or whatever it is, he becomes very strongly, forcefully attached to it, and you will see that they are not going to be human. You will not be able to sit down and talk to them. They are going to have a very fierce opposition to anything: they are on a holy mission. If you try to talk to them, they are not there.

sensitivity.reason: A generalisation about baalei teshuva: that without proper instruction they easily end up "not human", impossible to talk to.
sensitivity.publishable: A person whose whole approach to religion is *emuna*, with a big, passionate drive for altruism, can easily end up not being a person if he is not given proper instruction. If he connects that passion to just one aspect of the truth, he becomes very strongly, forcefully attached to it, and he is not going to be human. You will not be able to sit down and talk to him. He has a very fierce opposition to anything: he is on a holy mission. If you try to talk to him, he is not there.

blocks.text: As soon as you say something that is not what they want to hear, they get angry, and they start trying to put you down and even to insult you, because they want to invalidate your opinion; they do not care whether they do it by invalidating you or the actual thing. They already know that this is bad, so it does not matter how they get it away from you. It is not an issue of considering what the person is saying. So it is not really a healthy thing, and it is not very comfortable to be around. But that is not a person.

sensitivity.reason: Continues the generalisation about baalei teshuva who were not properly instructed.
sensitivity.publishable: As soon as you say something that is not what he wants to hear, he gets angry and tries to put you down, even to insult you, because he wants to invalidate your opinion; he does not care whether he does it by invalidating you or the actual thing. He already knows that this is bad. It is not an issue of considering what the person is saying. It is not a healthy thing. But that is not a person.

blocks.text: The *inyan* of a person means that you see a deeper will, and you see how all these *ratzonos* fit, so that I can see the other person's point of view. "I maybe think that practically, from the side of a *ratzon murkav*, this is better, but I can understand where he's coming from, and I also have a will for that."

That is also like the Baal Shem Tov's saying, that if you see a bad in somebody else, you really have it in yourself. Really, anything that you see in somebody else you have in yourself in some way. Every person really has all these *ratzonos*.

blocks.title: The truth, and the lower realms
blocks.text: A lot of times there are fights because people lock onto two different wills that are essential things, but inwardly they want the same thing. For example, there is the thing of *emuna*, and the whole thing of making a *dira b'tachtonim* (a dwelling below). Making a *dira b'tachtonim* means that you want to take the truth, the full truth of *Yiddishkeit*, and bring it down into the world, into the lower realms. A person could lock onto one of those two sides and say, "If it's going to be a *dira b'tachtonim*, you can't dilute the truth." And the other person can lock onto the fact that it has to be in the lower realms.

This is kind of like one person who is in the lights of *Tohu* and the vessels of *Tohu*, and one person in the lights of *Tikun* and the vessels of *Tikun*. One person lets go of the real goal just to compromise; another does not compromise his goal, but he is never going to accomplish it, because he is not willing to compromise on how he is going to do it. That happens a lot of times. Some people are very altruistic but not practical, and some people are practical. The real thing is that you have to realize that your goal is to bring it out, and so you have to do both.

blocks.title: From the yeshiva to mivtzaim
blocks.text: Rather, only in *Tikun*, when every *nekuda* comes out into *hispashtus*, outside its essence: **the *inyan* of a person is *davka* in a way of *Tikun***. You do not let the *nekuda* stay in its altruism. That is one of the differences: if you are a teenager sitting in *yeshiva*, it is very easy to be altruistic, but when you go out on *mivtzaim* (outreach), you have to be practical. If you want to start bringing somebody up, you cannot tell him, "Well, religion is an all-or-nothing thing. If you believe in Judaism, then you have to do everything it says; you can't pick and choose." That is really the truth: if this is what G-d wants me to do, I am going to do everything. But on the other hand, practically, you cannot have a person start doing everything.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 opens with the first half of line 46 (w0-59), read without the alignment's mark, which falls on the second half at w1201.

blocks.text: This is the same thing: the *mashal* we are using now is the *mashal* we were using for the *igulim*. The *igulim* are the way it is in hiddenness, and this is the way it comes out, revealed, in a particular thing. They correspond to each other. The difference is whether it is the essence itself or already for a particular; but it is the same thing we said there.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: That is what a person needs in order to bring it into *Tikun*, to make *hishtalshelus* (the chain of descent). But that does not mean that you drop that essential thing. You realize, that is my goal; but you write it down on a piece of paper and put it in your pocket. "Okay, I'm not forgetting that. But now, what is my practical goal?" If a person has a mature view, if he really wants to do what *Hashem* wants, he realizes that it is not hypocritical to take a baby step and do something that he will be able to do, practically. Because that is the only way he is ever going to do it.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: If he really wants it to happen, he has to. That is the thing it says: the *yetzer hara* gets a person to say, "No, I want to do everything. If I'm going to do it, I'm going to do it right, I'm going to be perfect." Why is that the *yetzer hara*? Because the *yetzer hara* comes from *Tohu*. The *yetzer hara* comes from a person saying that it is all or nothing.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: From the side of *chesed* of *Tohu* you say, "I have an essential connection to G-d. No matter what I do, G-d's going to be with me and He's going to love me, I'm going to be connected, so it doesn't matter what I do." That can come out to *kelipa* (what conceals G-dliness). That is the way *chesed* of *Tohu* becomes the root of the *kelipa* of Yishmael.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: The *gevura* of *Tohu* says, "No matter what I do, I'm never going to be able to act in a way that's good enough for G-d. I'm never going to be able to do the *mitzvos* perfectly, the way that's fitting for G-d, to express in an action the full glory that G-d deserves. It's never going to be perfect. No matter how good I'm going to be, 'there is no righteous man on earth'; I'm never going to really be able to reach G-d through that." So then he says, "Well, if I'm never going to be perfect, and there's always room to improve, then what's the point of ever starting?"
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: And this is the root of the *kelipa* of Esav, a *gevura* of *kelipa*. "I don't know that much about the Muslim philosophy, but Christianity, this is what they say." They say that it is true that G-d wants you to do the Torah and the *mitzvos*, and you should do them; but since it is so hard, it is impossible for you to do them without sinning, without messing up somewhere, and so you do not have to do any of them; instead, just rely on being saved by "Yoshke". That is what they say. So that is how, from the *gevura* of *kelipa*, came out a kind of *chesed*: "Well, you can just do whatever you want, really." The reason is that by nature they are so *gevura*-dik that they give up and say it does not matter what you do. So that is how they come out to the *kelipa*.

The reason is that by nature he is so *gevura*-dik that he gives up and says it does not matter what you do. That is how it comes out to the *kelipa*.

blocks.text: This is what the *yetzer hara* does to a person: it makes him altruistic, kind of, and makes him lock into one of these essential *middos*; and then that becomes debilitating, a lack of action. That is the *inyan* of a *ratzo* (running towards) without a *shov* (returning): he has this *ratzo* for the *Tohu*, which is good, but he is not focused on the result.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: If you are focused on the result, if your real inner essential will is that it should come down in practice, then you are always going to take these things and say, "How can I use this *chesed* of good to motivate me to do good?" The way to use it is to say: no matter how low I am, there is always some step I can do that will be meaningful, and I have value. So a person feels lifted up, no matter how little he is; he realizes that G-d treasures him, and that the little effort he puts in is worth as much to G-d as that of a big *tzaddik* (righteous person), because it is on his level. That is the way it comes into holiness.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: And the *gevura* side is that no matter how much I have accomplished, I can never be happy with what I accomplished, because there is always room to improve. That is the way you use those; that is the way Yitzchak and Yaakov used *chesed* and *gevura*. The difference is whether you are focused on what you are actually accomplishing, the bottom line, or not. If you are focusing on the bottom line, then it is of *Tikun*, a good thing; otherwise it is *Tohu*.

blocks.text: Then they are included together through the many vessels, the different vessels, in which they are combined: **when it comes out from the *etzem hanekuda* into *Tikun*, then all the opposite things are expressed, but they're expressed in a limited way, kind of**. You find some place for each of these things. That is the *inyan* of a *partzuf*: they are all expressed together because they are being limited, each expressed only in one example, a certain limited example. But then you can have them all together.

phrases.he: וזה מה שכתוב בספר יצירה
טרף אש ומים ובללן זה בזה
phrases.en: Take *eish u'mayim* and mix them together.

phrases.he: דהיינו בחינת המורכב דאש ומים דוקא, ולא בעצם מהותן כו' וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר באריכות:

blocks.text: And this is what is written in *Sefer Yetzira* (the Book of Formation): **Take *eish u'mayim* and mix them together**: that is the way *Hashem* made the world. The essential thing of fire and the essential thing of water are opposites, both physically and spiritually. But to have an actual physical world, those forms had to be combined. There is no physical thing that does not have some of the properties of both, that is purely fire or purely water. And the same thing spiritually.

That is, the composite of fire and water *davka* (specifically), and not in their very essence, as is explained elsewhere at length. When you come out to physical things, it is impossible to have one without the other. You are never going to find something that is completely, externally perfect, and you are never going to find something that has no merit. You always have both things.

reviewQuestions.question: What does it mean that each *sefira* of *Tohu* is a *nekuda*, and why does dividing each *sefira* into ten make *Tikun*?
Why is the person who reads Dale Carnegie's book not *chafetz chesed*, and what does the essential will for kindness have that his will lacks?
Why can two opposite essential wills not compromise, and what happens to the person who is "totally nice, always" or who says "get it yourself"?
Why could Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel not convince each other, and why is their dispute only half an example?
How is kindness to one who saved your life different from the kindness of a person who is kind by nature?
How could G-d punish Shaul and order his eulogy at the same time, and what does that show about the composite *middos* of *Tikun*?

Line 38's phrase cites his summing-up sentence (74 w1593-1608), and line 40's the English he gives right after reading it in class 75.

Shaul and the Givonim (74 w1151-1346): he says Shaul killed the Givonim "because they helped Dovid". In the verses (Shmuel II 21) the plague is for Shaul's killing of the Givonim; the link to helping Dovid comes through the city of Nov, whose kohanim gave Dovid food and whom the Givonim served (a Midrashic reading). The block keeps his words; a reviewer may want to check.
"Where His judgement is, there..." (74 w1106): he says he forgets the end of the verse; the block keeps it as an unfinished quotation.

"That's the way that Yitzchak and Yaakov used chesed and gevura" (76 w1138-1150): kept as he said it, though chesed and gevura are usually paired with Avraham and Yitzchak. A reviewer may want to check whether he misspoke. The next sentence's "the ratzui of Tikun" (76 w1173-1185) is unclear in the transcript and is rendered only as "it is of Tikun".

"The long short way and the short long way" (73 w1638-1776): he tells it without naming the source; it is the Gemara's story (Eruvin 53b) of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and a child at a crossroads, which he retells as a way to a palace. Kept as he tells it.

"One person in the lights of Tohu and the vessels of Tohu, one in the lights of Tikun and the vessels of Tikun" (75 w2183-2220): kept as he said it; the pairing with the two people that follow (the one who compromises the goal and the one who will not compromise the means) is not spelled out, and he may have meant lights of Tohu in vessels of Tikun.
